arXiv:2511.13422v2 [gr-qc] 23 Jun 2026

On the uniqueness of continuous spacetime extensions in 1+1-dimensions with applications to weak null singularities

Peter Cameron Note: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London, South Kensington Campus, London SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom and the Heilbronn Institute for Mathematical Research, Bristol, UK. Email: p.cameron24@imperial.ac.uk    & Jan Sbierski Note: School of Mathematics and Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Science, University of Edinburgh, James Clerk Maxwell Building, Peter Guthrie Tait Road, Edinburgh EH9 3FD, United Kingdom. Email: jan.sbierski@ed.ac.uk
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Motivated by weak null singularities in black hole interiors, we study 1+1-dimensional Lorentzian manifolds (M,g)(M,g) which admit a continuous spacetime extension across a null boundary v=0v=0, where v<0v<0 is a null coordinate. We study the degree to which such extensions are unique up to the boundary. Firstly, we find that in general not even the C0C^{0}-structure of the extension is uniquely determined by the assumption that the metric extends continuously. However, we exhibit an interesting local-global relation regarding the C0C^{0}-structure which in particular entails its rigidity for “strongly spherically symmetric” continuous extensions across the Cauchy horizon of the Reissner-Nordström spacetime. Secondly, we construct continuous extensions which have the same C0C^{0}-structure, but do not have equivalent C1C^{1}-structures. This construction also carries over to weak null singularities in 3+1-dimensions. Understanding the uniqueness properties of continuous spacetime extensions to the boundary is of importance for the study of low-regularity inextendibility problems [26].

1 Introduction

A weak null singularity is a singular null boundary of a spacetime (M,g)(M,g) solving the Einstein equations such that the metric is continuous up to the boundary but the Christoffel symbols fail to be square integrable. These are expected to form in the interior of generic rotating black holes. For a detailed background to weak null singularities we refer the reader to [19, 6, 26]. Here, we focus on a local piece (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) of the spacetime near the weak null singularity, where Mwns=(−1,1)×(−1,0)×𝕊2M_{\mathrm{wns}}=(-1,1)\times(-1,0)\times\mathbb{S}^{2} with coordinates (u,v)(u,v) on the first two factors and (θ1,θ2)=θA(\theta^{1},\theta^{2})=\theta^{A}, A=1,2A=1,2, an arbitrary set of smooth coordinates on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. The metric is given in the double null form

gwns=−Ω2​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)+γA​B​(d​θA−bA​d​v)⊗(d​θB−bB​d​v),g_{\mathrm{wns}}=-\Omega^{2}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+\gamma_{AB}(d\theta^{A}-b^{A}dv)\otimes(d\theta^{B}-b^{B}dv)\;, (1)

where Ω\Omega is a smooth strictly positive function on MwnsM_{\mathrm{wns}}, γ⁡(u,v)\gamma(u,v) is a smooth Riemannian metric on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} which depends smoothly on uu and vv, and b⁡(u,v)b(u,v) is a smooth vector field on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} which also depends smoothly on uu and vv. The time orientation is fixed by stipulating that ∂u\partial_{u} is future-directed null. The “weakness” of the singularity is signalled by the fact that the metric extends continuously to the singularity at {v=0}\{v=0\} with respect to the (u,v,θ1,θ2)(u,v,\theta^{1},\theta^{2})-differentiable structure. This means Ω\Omega, γA​B\gamma_{AB} and bAb^{A} extend continuously to Mwns¯:=(−1,1)×(−1,0]×𝕊2⊇Mwns\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}:=(-1,1)\times(-1,0]\times\mathbb{S}^{2}\supseteq M_{\mathrm{wns}} such that Ω\Omega is strictly positive and, for fixed uu and vv, γA​B\gamma_{AB} is a Riemannian metric on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} and bAb^{A} is a vector field on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. Note that {v=0}\{v=0\} is a null hypersurface. The existence of this continuous extension to {v=0}\{v=0\}, together with upper bounds on various Christoffel symbols, has been established in [6, Theorem 4.24]. Moreover, it is conjectured and expected (cf. [2, 6, 19, 24, 12] and references therein) that the metric gwnsg_{\mathrm{wns}} indeed becomes singular for v→0v\to 0 and that the Lorentzian manifold (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) is inextendible ‘across’ {v=0}\{v=0\} as a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric and locally square integrable Christoffel symbols. Here, it is helpful to recall the following definitions: consider a Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g), a regularity class Γ\Gamma (e.g. Γ=C0,Cloc0,1,C∞\Gamma=C^{0},C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}},C^{\infty}), and assume that the Lorentzian metric gg is at least Γ\Gamma-regular. In this paper, all manifolds themselves are assumed to be smooth. A Γ\Gamma-extension of a Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) consists of an isometric embedding ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of (M,g)(M,g) into a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) of the same dimension as MM where g~\tilde{g} is Γ\Gamma-regular and such that ∂ι⁡(M)⊂M~\partial\iota(M)\subset\tilde{M} is non-empty. If a Γ\Gamma-extension of (M,g)(M,g) exists, we say that (M,g)(M,g) is Γ\Gamma-extendible; otherwise we say (M,g)(M,g) is Γ\Gamma-inextendible. Returning to the particular case of the weak null singularity, a Γ\Gamma-extension of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} is a Γ\Gamma-extension ι:Mwns↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) such that there exists a future-directed causal curve τ:[−1,0)→Mwns\tau:[-1,0)\to M_{\mathrm{wns}} with lims→0τv​(s)=0\lim_{s\to 0}\tau_{v}(s)=0, lims→0τu​(s)<1\lim_{s\to 0}\tau_{u}(s)<1 and such that lims→0(ι∘τ)​(s)∈∂ι⁡(Mwns)⊂M~\lim_{s\to 0}(\iota\circ\tau)(s)\in\partial\iota(M_{\mathrm{wns}})\subset\tilde{M} exists.

We are interested in the local uniqueness of continuous extensions ι:Mwns↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) across {v=0}\{v=0\}. We ask the following question: suppose lims→0τ⁡(s)=(u∗,0,ω∗)∈Mwns¯\lim_{s\to 0}\tau(s)=(u_{*},0,\omega_{*})\in\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}, does there exist ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and a small neighbourhood B𝕊2B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} of ω∗\omega_{*} in 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} such that ι|(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)×B𝕊2:(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)×B𝕊2→M~\iota|_{(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}}:(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\to\tilde{M} extends to

ι¯:(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0]×B𝕊2→M~\overline{\iota}:(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0]\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\to\tilde{M}

as a C1C^{1}-diffeomorphism (or at least as a homeomorphism) onto its image? If the answer is positive, then we say that ι:Mwns↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is locally C1C^{1}-(C0C^{0}-)equivalent to Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}} at (u∗,0,ω∗)∈Mwns¯(u_{*},0,\omega_{*})\in\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}} and it is easy to see that this notion is independent of the curve τ\tau that approaches (u∗,0,ω∗)(u_{*},0,\omega_{*}). If the answer is negative, we say that ι:Mwns↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is locally C1C^{1}-(C0C^{0}-)inequivalent to Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}} at (u∗,0,ω∗)∈Mwns¯(u_{*},0,\omega_{*})\in\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}.

Paraphrasing the above question, we have already found one continuous extension of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} by extending the topological and differentiable structure of Mwns=(−1,1)×(−1,0)×𝕊2∋(u,v,θA)M_{\mathrm{wns}}=(-1,1)\times(-1,0)\times\mathbb{S}^{2}\ni(u,v,\theta^{A}) to Mwns¯=(−1,1)×(−1,0]×𝕊2∋(u,v,θA)\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}=(-1,1)\times(-1,0]\times\mathbb{S}^{2}\ni(u,v,\theta^{A}). Can one extend the topological and/or differentiable structure of MwnsM_{\mathrm{wns}} differently and still obtain a continuous extension across {v=0}\{v=0\}?

The relevance of this local uniqueness question is twofold. Firstly, it arises naturally in low-regularity inextendibility proofs. For example, in the proof of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of spherically symmetric weak null singularities [23], which is based on the blow-up of a local holonomy, it is crucial to control the velocity vectors of a sequence of curves in the local coordinates of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. That is, one needs a priori control on the C1C^{1}-differentiable structure of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. This would be provided by the statement above that ι|(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)×B𝕊2\iota|_{(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}} extends as a C1C^{1}-diffeomorphism to {v=0}\{v=0\}.11 1 In the paper [23] a slightly weaker statement is proved, which is, however, still sufficient for the application. Furthermore, recent work by the second author [26], combined with [25], shows that for hypothetical Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions of weak null singularities without any symmetry assumptions, ι|(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)×B𝕊2\iota|_{(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}} indeed extends as a C1C^{1}-diffeomorphism to {v=0}\{v=0\}, thus exactly providing this a priori control of the C1C^{1}-differentiable structure. If curvature is assumed to blow-up in a particular frame – note that a frame is an object at the level of the C1C^{1}-differentiable structure – then one can show that this is in contradiction to the metric extending in Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}. For showing that the hypothetical Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension is locally C1C^{1}-equivalent to Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}, one crucially uses, in addition to bounds on various connection coefficients, the local Lipschitz regularity of the extension. Hence, the local uniqueness question posed in this paper asks whether this a priori control on the C1C^{1}-differentiable structure can still be obtained for a C0C^{0}-extension. Understanding this question informs and constrains approaches to proving inextendibility of weak null singularities in regularity classes below Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}} (and above C0C^{0}). Ideally, one would like to prove inextendibility with a continuous metric and locally square integrable Christoffel symbols.

The second motivation for studying the local uniqueness of continuous extensions to weak null singularities stems from the old question in general relativity which asks what kind of structure one can associate to a spacetime singularity. The problem with this of course is that the singularity itself is usually not part of the spacetime. This prompted the development of various ideal boundary constructions [10, 9, 27, 28] (or [1] for a review) which assign various structures (causality, topology, etc.) to the singularity. The case of weak singularities is, however, fundamentally different in the sense that the spacetime, that is, the manifold with continuous metric, can be defined at the singularity. This naturally provides a causal, topological, and even differentiable structure. However, it has not yet been investigated whether these structures are uniquely determined by the property that the singularity admits one continuous extension, i.e., whether they are independent of the continuous extension chosen.

1.1 Previous results

The first systematic study of the uniqueness of at least Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions to Cloc2,1C^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}} boundaries was, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, carried out in [4]. It was shown that if two such extensions terminate the same null geodesic (i.e. if they are anchored by the same null geodesic), then locally they have the same Cloc2,1C^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}} differentiable structure. In [25] it was shown that if two Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions ιi:M↪M~i\iota_{i}:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) (without any further regularity assumptions on the boundary) are anchored by the same causal curve τ:[−1,0)→M\tau:[-1,0)\to M, then locally they have the same Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-differentiable structure. This can be phrased mathematically as follows: if lims→0(ιi∘τ)​(s)=:p~i∈∂ιi​(M)⊂M~i\lim_{s\to 0}(\iota_{i}\circ\tau)(s)=:\tilde{p}_{i}\in\partial\iota_{i}(M)\subset\tilde{M}_{i}, then there exist small neighbourhoods W~i⊂M~i\tilde{W}_{i}\subset\tilde{M}_{i} of p~i\tilde{p}_{i} which are divided into two parts, (W~i)<(\tilde{W}_{i})_{<} and (W~i)>(\tilde{W}_{i})_{>}, by a Lipschitz graph (W~i)=(\tilde{W}_{i})_{=} which lies in ∂ιi​(M)\partial\iota_{i}(M), contains p~i\tilde{p}_{i} and is such that (W~i)<(\tilde{W}_{i})_{<} lies in ιi​(M)\iota_{i}(M). The statement is then that the identification map id:=ι2∘ι1−1|ι1​(M):ι1​(M)→ι2​(M)\mathrm{id}:=\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1}^{-1}|_{\iota_{1}(M)}:\iota_{1}(M)\to\iota_{2}(M), restricted to (W~1)<(\tilde{W}_{1})_{<}, maps (W~1)<(\tilde{W}_{1})_{<} diffeomorphically to (W~2)<(\tilde{W}_{2})_{<} and extends as a Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-diffeomorphism to (W~1)≤:=(W~1)<∪(W~1)=(\tilde{W}_{1})_{\leq}:=(\tilde{W}_{1})_{<}\cup(\tilde{W}_{1})_{=}.

The local uniqueness question for continuous extensions of weak null singularities (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) in this paper is of exactly the same form: one may trivially extend the continuous boundary extension (Mwns¯,gwns)(\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) to a continuous extension ι1:Mwns↪(−1,1)×(−1,1)×𝕊2=:M~1\iota_{1}:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow(-1,1)\times(-1,1)\times\mathbb{S}^{2}=:\tilde{M}_{1} in the sense defined above by extending the metric to be constant in the (u,v,θA)(u,v,\theta^{A})-coordinates for v≥0v\geq 0. Let now ι2:Mwns↪M~2\iota_{2}:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}_{2} be another C0C^{0}-extension across {v=0}\{v=0\}. Then, considering MwnsM_{\mathrm{wns}} as a subset of M~1\tilde{M}_{1}, the identification map is id=ι2\mathrm{id}=\iota_{2} and we can choose W~1\tilde{W}_{1} such that (W~1)<=(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)×B𝕊2(\tilde{W}_{1})_{<}=(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} and (W~1)≤=(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0]×B𝕊2(\tilde{W}_{1})_{\leq}=(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0]\times B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}. The difference between this paper and the previous work mentioned above is that we have fixed a particular reference C0C^{0}-extension Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}}.22 2 To be precise, (Mwns¯,gwns)(\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) is not a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) in the sense defined earlier, since (Mwns¯,gwns)(\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) is a manifold with boundary, whereas an extension is defined to be an isometric embedding into a manifold without boundary. Hence it is more accurate to call (Mwns¯,gwns)(\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) a continuous boundary extension of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}). However, as noted above, a proper reference C0C^{0}-extension ι1:Mwns↪M~1\iota_{1}:M_{\mathrm{wns}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}_{1} may be constructed from this.

Furthermore, it is shown in [25] that local uniqueness fails in general for anchored extensions which are only Hölder continuous. This is done by constructing a counterexample in which the identification map extends as a homeomorphism but not as a C1C^{1}-diffeomorphism. However, the non-uniqueness mechanism of the counterexample does not transfer to the case of weak null singularities. The counterexample in [25] is 1+1-dimensional. In a double null gauge it is of the form M={(u,v)∈ℝ2|u+v>0}M=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\;|\;u+v>0\}, g=−Ω2​(u+v)​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)g=-\Omega^{2}(u+v)(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du) with Ω2​(u+v)→0\Omega^{2}(u+v)\to 0 for u+v→0u+v\to 0, and uses the fact that the boundary, which is null (!) in the extension, can be tangentially approached by either the left or right going null geodesics in the original spacetime. This is qualitatively different from the weak null singularities we are interested in, where the boundary in the reference C0C^{0}-extension is the limit of the family of null hypersurfaces {v=const}\{v=\mathrm{const}\}. Hence this example does not necessarily inform us about what might be expected in the case of weak null singularities.

1.2 A 1+1-dimensional toy model

The local uniqueness problem for continuous extensions in 3+1-dimensions, as set out earlier, is a very intricate problem about which literally nothing is known to the best knowledge of the authors. As a first step towards the resolution of this problem we begin in this paper by studying the following instructive 1+1-dimensional toy problem: we consider Mt:=(−1,1)×(−1,0)M_{t}:=(-1,1)\times(-1,0) with coordinates (u,v)(u,v) and metric gt=−Ω2​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)g_{t}=-\Omega^{2}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du), where Ω\Omega is a smooth strictly positive function on MtM_{t} which extends continuously as a strictly positive function to Mt¯:=(−1,1)×(−1,0]⊇Mt\overline{M_{t}}:=(-1,1)\times(-1,0]\supseteq M_{t}. A time orientation is fixed by stipulating that ∂u\partial_{u} is future-directed null. Now, given a continuous extension ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) and a future-directed causal C1C^{1}-curve τ:[−1,0)→Mt\tau:[-1,0)\to M_{t} with lims→0τu​(s)=:u∗<1\lim_{s\to 0}\tau_{u}(s)=:u_{*}<1, lims→0τv​(s)=0\lim_{s\to 0}\tau_{v}(s)=0 and such that lims→0(ι∘τ)​(s)∈∂ι⁡(Mt)⊂M~\lim_{s\to 0}(\iota\circ\tau)(s)\in\partial\iota(M_{t})\subset\tilde{M} exists33 3 As before, a continuous extension ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} with these properties is called a C0C^{0}-extension across {v=0}\{v=0\}., we ask whether there is an ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that ι|(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0)→M~\iota|_{(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0)}\to\tilde{M} extends to

ι¯:(u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ)×(−ϵ,0]→M~\begin{split}\overline{\iota}:(u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon)\times(-\epsilon,0]\to\tilde{M}\end{split} (2)

as a C1C^{1}-diffeomorphism/homeomorphism onto its image. Again, if the answer is positive, then we say that ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is locally C1C^{1}-(C0C^{0}-)equivalent to Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} at (u∗,0)∈Mt¯(u_{*},0)\in\overline{M_{t}} and it is easy to see that this notion is independent of the curve τ\tau that approaches (u∗,0)(u_{*},0). If the answer is negative, we say that ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is locally C1C^{1}-(C0C^{0}-)inequivalent to Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} at (u∗,0)∈Mt¯(u_{*},0)\in\overline{M_{t}}. This follows the definitions made in 3+1-dimensions.

1.3 Main results

The main results of our investigation are contained in Section 4, which discusses the C0C^{0}-structure of extensions, and Section 5, which looks at the C1C^{1}-structure. Recall that we consider the 1+1-dimensional model spacetime Mt=(−1,1)×(−1,0)M_{t}=(-1,1)\times(-1,0) with smooth metric gt=−Ω2​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)g_{t}=-\Omega^{2}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du) under the assumption that Ω\Omega extends as a continuous strictly positive function to Mt¯=(−1,1)×(−1,0]\overline{M_{t}}=(-1,1)\times(-1,0], which defines our reference extension. In Example 4.1, under the additional assumption that Ω\Omega extends continuously as a strictly positive function to [−1,1]×(−1,0][-1,1]\times(-1,0], we construct a whole family of C0C^{0}-extensions of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} which terminate all future-directed null curves of constant uu at the same point! We refer to such extensions as corner extensions. They are clearly not locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension Mt¯\overline{M_{t}}. A natural question is now whether it is also possible for a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} to terminate only a subset of constant uu curves at the same point and to terminate the remaining constant uu curves at different boundary points. Proposition 4.2 shows that, under our assumptions on Ω\Omega, this is not possible: if two nearby curves of constant uu terminate at the same point, then all other curves of constant uu must also terminate at this point.44 4 See Proposition 4.2 for the precise statement. It is important to assume that the two curves of constant uu approach the same boundary point from the same null direction in the extension – and not, say, one from the future and one from the past with respect to a small neighbourhood of the boundary point in question. Such extensions may be constructed, but they do not resemble a corner extension. In particular, this local assumption on nearby curves of constant uu fixes the global structure of the C0C^{0}-extension. We then conclude in Theorem 4.3 that a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} is either locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} or has the global C0C^{0}-structure of a corner extension. This classifies the possible local C0C^{0}-structures of such extensions.

Next, we focus on the corner extensions and ask whether they are also relevant for C0C^{0}-extensions to weak null singularities in 3+1-dimensions. More specifically, we study a class of C0C^{0}-extensions across the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon which preserve spherical symmetry. Considering the quotient spacetime induced by the spherical symmetry of subextremal Reissner-Nordström (or more generally by a spherically symmetric weak null singularity), we obtain a 1+1-dimensional Lorentzian manifold. By considering extensions of this manifold separately, and extending the 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} identically, one obtains a strongly spherically symmetric extension of the original 3+1-dimensional spacetime (see Section 4.2.1). Working in Kruskal coordinates (U,V)(U,V), a finite UU-chunk of this Lorentzian manifold is of the form (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) and thus we may indeed construct a corner extension as in Example 4.1 (see Section 4.2). Moreover, since the area radius rr in exact subextremal Reissner-Nordström is constant on the Cauchy horizon, this corner extension can even be constructed in 3+1-dimensions, see Example 4.5.55 5 For generic spherically symmetric weak null singularities rr is strictly monotonically decreasing in uu and thus this local construction is not possible. However, this construction is only possible for C0C^{0}-extensions of a subset of the Reissner-Nordström spacetime of finite UU-coordinate, see Corollary 4.6. If we consider the quotient spacetime globally, then it is shown in Proposition 4.4 and Corollary 4.6 that, due to the infinite spacetime volume between the event horizon and Cauchy horizon, no such corner extension can exist. It thus follows that every strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extension across the Cauchy horizon is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension. To summarise, the possibility of the C0C^{0}-structure of a corner extension as in Theorem 4.3 disappears for global reasons if one considers strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extensions of the global spacetime – thus leaving only the familiar local C0C^{0}-structure of the reference extension.

Having understood the rigidity of the local C0C^{0}-structure of C0C^{0}-extensions of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across {v=0}\{v=0\}, in Section 5 we investigate whether there is any rigidity for the C1C^{1}-structure. Example 5.1 shows there are different corner extensions with non-equivalent C1C^{1}-structures. In Example 5.2 we construct a C0C^{0}-extension which has the same C0C^{0}-structure as the reference extension Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} but inequivalent C1C^{1}-structure. This shows there is no rigidity at the level of the C1C^{1}-structure. Moreover, the construction from Example 5.2 also generalises to weak null singularities in 3+1-dimensions without any symmetry assumptions. In particular, in Example 5.3 we construct a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mw​n​s,gw​n​s)(M_{wns},g_{wns}) across {v=0}\{v=0\} which is C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}} constructed by Dafermos and Luk in [6] but C1C^{1}-inequivalent!

1.4 Outline of paper

In Section 2 we lay down some further definitions, recall some basic results on near Minkowski neighbourhoods and causal homotopies, and slightly strengthen them in 1+1-dimensions. Furthermore, as an auxiliary result needed for the next section, we prove in Proposition 2.6 that, in 1+1-dimensions, a locally Lipschitz causal curve which is achronal with respect to smooth timelike curves can be reparameterised as a C1C^{1} null curve. The main result of Section 3 is Proposition 3.2. We show that ϵ>0\epsilon>0 can be chosen so that ι¯\overline{\iota} defined in (2) is continuous. This can be thought of as the statement that the reference extension has the “richest” possible C0C^{0}-structure in the sense that it adds the most boundary points. Another important property established in Proposition 3.2 is that if the boundary corresponding to {v=0}\{v=0\} is not a single point (as in the case of a corner extension), then this part of the boundary is a C1C^{1} null curve which is transverse to the curves of constant uu. Starting from this a priori description of the boundary, we then investigate the local C0C^{0}- and C1C^{1}-structures of C0C^{0}-extensions in Sections 4 and 5 as discussed above.

2 Definitions and Background Results

Throughout this paper we will rely on a number of definitions and technical results which we collect in this section. Following [11] (see in particular Lemma 2.7), given a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g), we define

I±​(p,M):={q∈M:∃ future/past-directed piecewise smooth timelike curve from p to q}J±​(p,M):={q∈M:∃ future/past-directed locally Lipschitz causal curve from p to q}.\begin{split}I^{\pm}(p,M)&:=\{q\in M:\exists\text{ future/past-directed {piecewise smooth} timelike curve from $p$ to $q$}\}\\ J^{\pm}(p,M)&:=\{q\in M:\exists\text{ future/past-directed {locally Lipschitz} causal curve from $p$ to $q$}\}.\end{split} (3)

The definition of a (future/past-directed) locally Lipschitz causal curve follows [3, Definition 1.3], see also [11, Definition 2.3]. Unless otherwise stated, all causal curves are assumed to be locally Lipschitz and all timelike curves are assumed to be piecewise smooth. This definition ensures that, for g∈C0g\in C^{0}, I±​(p,M)I^{\pm}(p,M) is open [11, Lemma 2.7] and the accumulation curve result [3, Theorem 1.6] holds for causal curves.

It will often be convenient to reparameterise causal curves by different smooth time functions, in which case the following Lemma will be useful.

Lemma 2.1.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg, let γ:[0,1]→M\gamma:[0,1]\to M be a future (or past) directed locally Lipschitz causal curve, and let tt be a smooth time function on MM. Then γ\gamma can be reparameterised by tt and we denote this reparameterisation by γ(1)\overset{(1)}{\gamma}. If γ\gamma is differentiable at s0∈[0,1]s_{0}\in[0,1] with non-vanishing causal derivative at this point, then γ(1)\overset{(1)}{\gamma} is differentiable at t⁡(γ⁡(s0))t\big(\gamma(s_{0})\big). Furthermore, if γ\gamma is C1C^{1} near s0s_{0} with non-vanishing causal derivative at this point then γ(1)\overset{(1)}{\gamma} is C1C^{1} near t⁡(γ⁡(s0))t\big(\gamma(s_{0})\big).

Proof.

Since γ\gamma is locally Lipschitz and tt is smooth, we have that s​↦𝜎​t​(γ⁡(s))s\overset{\sigma}{\mapsto}t\big(\gamma(s)\big) is locally Lipschitz and thus for 0≤s1<s2≤10\leq s_{1}<s_{2}\leq 1 we have

σ⁡(s2)−σ⁡(s1)=∫s1s2σ′​(s)​𝑑s=∫s1s2d​t​(γ′​(s))​𝑑s>0,\sigma(s_{2})-\sigma(s_{1})=\int_{s_{1}}^{s_{2}}\sigma^{\prime}(s)\,ds=\int_{s_{1}}^{s_{2}}dt\big(\gamma^{\prime}(s)\big)\,ds>0\;,

where in the last inequality we have assumed that γ\gamma is future-directed – if it were past-directed, we would get the reverse inequality. In either case it follows that s​↦𝜎​t​(γ⁡(s))s\overset{\sigma}{\mapsto}t\big(\gamma(s)\big) is strictly monotonic, which implies that it can be inverted and thus γ\gamma can be reparameterised by tt. Moreover, since tt is a smooth time function and γ\gamma is differentiable at s0s_{0} with non-vanishing causal derivative at this point, it follows that σ\sigma is differentiable at s0s_{0} with non-vanishing derivative there. Hence the inverse function σ−1\sigma^{-1} is differentiable at t0:=t⁡(γ⁡(s0))t_{0}:=t\big(\gamma(s_{0})\big). Thus, γ(1)​(t):=γ⁡(σ−1​(t))\overset{(1)}{\gamma}(t):=\gamma\big(\sigma^{-1}(t)\big) is differentiable at t0t_{0}. If γ\gamma is C1C^{1} near s0s_{0} then the same argument shows that σ\sigma is C1C^{1} near s0s_{0} and hence σ−1\sigma^{-1} is C1C^{1} near t0t_{0}. It follows that γ(1)\overset{(1)}{\gamma} is C1C^{1} near t0t_{0}. ∎

A useful notion which is used extensively in [8], [21], and [25] is that of the future boundary.

Definition 2.4.

[8, Definition 2.1] Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional Lorentzian manifold with g∈C0g\in C^{0} and let ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a C0C^{0}-extension of MM. The future boundary of MM is the set ∂+ι⁡(M)\partial^{+}\iota(M) consisting of all points p~∈M~\tilde{p}\in\tilde{M} such that there exists a smooth timelike curve γ~:[−1,0]→M~\tilde{\gamma}:[-1,0]\rightarrow\tilde{M} with Im(γ~|[−1,0))⊂ι(M)Im\left(\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)}\right)\subset\iota(M), γ~​(0)=p~∈∂ι⁡(M)\tilde{\gamma}(0)=\tilde{p}\in\partial\iota(M), and ι−1∘γ~|[−1,0)\iota^{-1}\circ\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)} is future-directed in MM.

It is clear that ∂+ι⁡(M)⊂∂ι⁡(M)\partial^{+}\iota(M)\subset\partial\iota(M). Throughout this paper we will abuse notation and write e.g. γ~|[−1,0)\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)} for Im(γ~|[−1,0))Im(\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)}) when referring to images of curves. Under the additional assumption that (M,g)(M,g) is globally hyperbolic, one can obtain the following result for points in the future boundary ∂+ι⁡(M)\partial^{+}\iota(M).

Proposition 2.5.

[25, Proposition 2.3] Let ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a C0C^{0}-extension of a time-oriented globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) with g∈C0g\in C^{0} and with Cauchy hypersurface Σ\Sigma. Let p~∈∂+ι⁡(M)\tilde{p}\in\partial^{+}\iota(M). Then, for every δ>0\delta>0, in addition to choosing a corresponding near Minkowski neighbourhood φ~:U~→(−ϵ0,ϵ0)×(−ϵ1,ϵ1)d\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{U}\rightarrow(-\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{0})\times(-\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{1})^{d}, ϵ0,ϵ1>0\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{1}>0, centred at p~\tilde{p}, there exists a Lipschitz continuous function f:(−ϵ1,ϵ1)d→(−ϵ0,ϵ0)f:(-\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{1})^{d}\rightarrow(-\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{0}) with the following property:

U~<:={(x0,x¯)∈(−ϵ0,ϵ0)×(−ϵ1,ϵ1)d:x0<f⁡(x¯)}⊂φ~​(ι⁡(I+​(Σ,M))∩U~)\tilde{U}_{<}:=\{(x_{0},\underline{x})\in(-\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{0})\times(-\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{1})^{d}:x_{0}<f(\underline{x})\}\subset\tilde{\varphi}(\iota(I^{+}(\Sigma,M))\cap\tilde{U}) (16)

and

{(x0,x¯)∈(−ϵ0,ϵ0)×(−ϵ1,ϵ1)d:x0=f⁡(x¯)}⊂φ~​(∂+ι⁡(M)∩U~).\{(x_{0},\underline{x})\in(-\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{0})\times(-\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{1})^{d}:x_{0}=f(\underline{x})\}\subset\tilde{\varphi}(\partial^{+}\iota(M)\cap\tilde{U}). (17)

Moreover, the set on the left hand side of (17), i.e. the graph of ff, is achronal (with respect to smooth timelike curves) in U~\tilde{U}.

We refer to (U~,φ~)(\tilde{U},\tilde{\varphi}) as a future boundary chart centred at p~\tilde{p}. It will also be convenient to define

U~≤:={φ~−1​(x0,x¯)∈U~:x0≤f⁡(x¯)}.\tilde{U}_{\leq}:=\{\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(x_{0},\underline{x})\in\tilde{U}:x_{0}\leq f(\underline{x})\}. (18)

Remark 2.7.

In [15] it was shown that if the metric is C0,1C^{0,1} then causal maximisers admit a C1,1C^{1,1} parameterisation, while if the metric is C0,αC^{0,\alpha} (α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)) then they admit only a C1,α4C^{1,\frac{\alpha}{4}} parameterisation. Proposition 2.6 shows that, in two spacetime dimensions, if the metric is C0C^{0} then null maximisers admit a C1C^{1} parameterisation.

The following lemma concerns the 1+1-dimensional spacetime (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) from Section 1.2 and will also be used in the proof of Proposition 3.2.

Lemma 2.10.

3 First Structural Properties of Extensions in 1+1-Dimensions

The aim of this section is to start the investigation of the local structure of the boundary ∂ι⁡(Mt)\partial\iota(M_{t}), where ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is a C0C^{0}-extension across {v=0}\{v=0\} of the two dimensional Lorentzian manifold (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) introduced in Section 1.2. In Proposition 3.2 we will show that, locally, ι\iota extends continuously to the boundary of M¯t\overline{M}_{t}. Moreover, we make a special choice of near Minkowski coordinates centred at a point on the boundary ∂ι⁡(Mt)\partial\iota(M_{t}) which may be considered as introducing a ‘normal form’ for such continuous extensions. Various general properties of such C0C^{0}-extensions with respect to these coordinates will be collated, which will be used in the following sections. We define γu0\gamma^{u_{0}} to be the curve u=u0u=u_{0} in MtM_{t} (parameterised by vv) and λv0\lambda^{v_{0}} to be the curve v=v0v=v_{0} (parameterised by uu). We also define γ~u0:=ι∘γu0\tilde{\gamma}^{u_{0}}:=\iota\circ\gamma^{u_{0}} and λ~v0:=ι∘λv0\tilde{\lambda}^{v_{0}}:=\iota\circ\lambda^{v_{0}}. Furthermore, we recall the following definition:

Definition 3.1.

[5, Definition 2.6.3] Let μn:I→M\mu_{n}:I\rightarrow M, n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, be a sequence of continuous curves in (M,g)(M,g), where g∈C0g\in C^{0}. We shall say that μ:I→M\mu:I\rightarrow M is an accumulation curve of the μn\mu_{n}’s, or that the μn\mu_{n}’s accumulate at μ\mu, if there exists a subsequence of (μn)n=1∞(\mu_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} that converges to μ\mu uniformly (with respect to local coordinates) on compact subsets of II.

Proposition 3.2.

We have so far seen two different local C0C^{0}-structures for C0C^{0}-extensions across v=0v=0 of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}). These are given by Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} from Section 1.2 and ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β\iota_{corner,\beta} from Example 4.1. In Theorem 4.3 we show that these are the only two possible local C0C^{0}-structures for such extensions. The proof relies on Proposition 4.2, which implies a rigidity property on the C0C^{0}-structure of the corner extension: if a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across v=0v=0 locally exhibits the C0C^{0}-structure of the corner extension, then it must do so globally. Theorem 4.3.

Let ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) such that p~u∗:=limv→0(ι∘γu∗)​(v)∈∂ι⁡(M)\tilde{p}_{u_{*}}:=\lim_{v\to 0}(\iota\circ\gamma^{u_{*}})(v)\in\partial\iota(M) exists for some u∗∈(−1,1)u_{*}\in(-1,1). Then one of the following holds:

  1. (a)

    ι\iota extends continuously to ι:(−1,1)×(−1,0]→M~\iota:(-1,1)\times(-1,0]\to\tilde{M} with ι⁡(u,0)=p~u∗\iota(u,0)=\tilde{p}_{u_{*}} for all u∈(−1,1)u\in(-1,1).

  2. (b)

    p~u∗∈∂+ι⁡(Mt)\tilde{p}_{u_{*}}\in\partial^{+}\iota(M_{t}) and there exist v∗<0<ϵv_{*}<0<\epsilon such that ι\iota extends to ι:[u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ]×[v∗,0]→U~≤\iota:[u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon]\times[v_{*},0]\to\tilde{U}_{\leq} as a homeomorphism onto its image, where (U~,φ~=(x~0,x~1))\big(\tilde{U},\tilde{\varphi}=(\tilde{x}_{0},\tilde{x}_{1})\big) is a future boundary chart centred at p~u∗\tilde{p}_{u_{*}}.

In particular, if we are not in case (a)(a) then the C0C^{0}-extension ι:Mt↪M~\iota:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} at (u∗,0)∈Mt¯(u_{*},0)\in\overline{M_{t}} and the conclusions of Proposition 3.2 (b) apply.

Proof.

By Proposition 3.2 (a)(i), we can choose a near Minkowski neighbourhood centred at p~u∗\tilde{p}_{u_{*}} as well as v∗<0<ϵv_{*}<0<\epsilon such that (33) holds on ι⁡([u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ]×[v∗,0))\iota([u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon]\times[v_{*},0)) and ι\iota extends continuously to ι:[u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ]×[v∗,0]↪U~\iota:[u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon]\times[v_{*},0]\hookrightarrow\tilde{U}. If ι⁡(u−,0)=ι⁡(u+,0)\iota(u_{-},0)=\iota(u_{+},0) for some u−,u+∈[u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ]u_{-},u_{+}\in[u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon] with u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} then by Proposition 4.2, ι\iota extends continuously to ι:(−1,1)×(−1,0]→M~\iota:(-1,1)\times(-1,0]\to\tilde{M} with ι⁡(u,0)=p~u∗\iota(u,0)=\tilde{p}_{u_{*}} for all u∈(−1,1)u\in(-1,1). Otherwise, ι:[u∗−ϵ,u∗+ϵ]×[v∗,0]↪U~\iota:[u_{*}-\epsilon,u_{*}+\epsilon]\times[v_{*},0]\hookrightarrow\tilde{U} is injective and thus a bijection onto its image. Since it is continuous and defined on a compact set, its inverse is also continuous [20, Theorem 4.17]. The remaining properties follow from Remark 3.3. ∎

Theorem 4.3 constitutes the first main result of this paper. It classifies the possible local C0C^{0}-structures of C0C^{0}-extensions of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) across {v=0}\{v=0\}: either the C0C^{0}-structure is locally equivalent to that of the reference extension Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} or all future-directed null curves of constant uu extend to the same point. In this paper, we have only obtained this classification in 1+1-dimensions. Nevertheless, this is sufficient for exploring strongly spherically symmetric extensions (defined below) of black hole interiors to Cauchy horizons in 3+1-dimensions. This is addressed in the next section.

4.2 Ruling out corner extensions from global structure

In Example 4.1 we constructed a corner extension across {v=0}\{v=0\} of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) – a C0C^{0}-extension such that ι⁡(u,0)=p~\iota(u,0)=\tilde{p} for all u∈(−1,1)u\in(-1,1). This construction required the extra assumption that Ω\Omega extends continuously to {u=±1}\{u=\pm 1\} as a strictly positive function.

In this section we leave our local toy spacetime (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) behind (recall this was a toy example describing a finite uu-piece of a weak null singularity or of a Cauchy horizon). We now consider a toy spacetime which models the entire weak null singularity or Cauchy horizon to the past. That is, we consider the 1+1-dimensional Lorentzian manifold (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}), where Q=(−∞,0)×(−∞,0)Q=(-\infty,0)\times(-\infty,0) with global coordinates (U,V)(U,V),

gQ=−Ω​(U,V)2​(d​U⊗d​V+d​V⊗d​U)g_{Q}=-\Omega(U,V)^{2}(dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU) (65)

and Ω\Omega is a smooth, strictly positive function on QQ which extends to Q¯:=(−∞,0)×(−∞,0]\overline{Q}:=(-\infty,0)\times(-\infty,0] as a continuous, strictly positive function.1515 15 The extension of the VV-domain from (−1,0)(-1,0) to (−∞,0)(-\infty,0) is of no importance for the result in this section. This is motivated by the study of strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extensions of the subextremal Reissner Nordström spacetime across the Cauchy horizon (see Section 4.2.1 for further discussion). In view of the rigidity of corner extensions exhibited in Proposition 4.2, in this section we show that the global structure of (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}) can rule out case (a)(a) in Theorem 4.3 even for local extensions.

Observe that for any −∞<U1<U2<0-\infty<U_{1}<U_{2}<0, Example 4.1 allows us to construct a corner extension across {V=0}\{V=0\} of the “finite UU-chunk” Q∗:=(U1,U2)×(−∞,0)⊂QQ^{*}:=(U_{1},U_{2})\times(-\infty,0)\subset Q. Indeed, consider (Q∗,gQ)(Q^{*},g_{Q}) with reference extension Q∗¯:=(U1,U2)×(−∞,0]\overline{Q^{*}}:=(U_{1},U_{2})\times(-\infty,0]. Rescaling UU and VV puts us in the setting of Example 4.1 and we thus obtain a C0C^{0}-extension ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β:Q∗↪Q~\iota_{corner,\beta}:Q^{*}\hookrightarrow\tilde{Q} with ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β​(U,0)=p~∈Q~\iota_{corner,\beta}(U,0)=\tilde{p}\in\tilde{Q} for all U∈(U1,U2)U\in(U_{1},U_{2}).

We now ask whether this construction can be “globalised” to construct a corner extension of the full (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}) across {V=0}\{V=0\}. The following example gives a condition which can be used to rule out the existence of such a global corner extension. It is based on the simple observation that, due to the local nature of the corner region, infinite spacetime volumes cannot be isometrically embedded into such regions.

Proposition 4.4.

Let ι\iota be a C0C^{0}-extension of (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}) to (Q~,g~Q~)(\tilde{Q},\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}) such that p~:=limV→0ι⁡(U∗,V)∈Q~\tilde{p}:=\lim_{V\rightarrow 0}\iota(U_{*},V)\in\tilde{Q} exists for some U∗∈(−∞,0)U_{*}\in(-\infty,0). In particular, ι\iota is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to Q¯\overline{Q} at (U∗,0)∈Q¯(U_{*},0)\in\overline{Q}.

Proof.

For large K>0K>0 consider the subregion (U∗−K,−1K)×(−∞,0)⊂Q(U_{*}-K,-\frac{1}{K})\times(-\infty,0)\subset Q. Let (U~,φ~=(x~0,x~1))(\tilde{U},\tilde{\varphi}=(\tilde{x}_{0},\tilde{x}_{1})) be a near Minkowski neighbourhood of p~\tilde{p}. By Proposition 4.2, there exists B~⊂U~\tilde{B}\subset\tilde{U} and V∗<0V_{*}<0 such that ι⁡((U∗−K,−1K)×(V∗,0))⊂B~\iota\big((U_{*}-K,-\frac{1}{K})\times(V_{*},0)\big)\subset\tilde{B}, cf. Figure 15. Since U~\tilde{U} is a near Minkowski neighbourhood, working in the geometry of (Q~,g~Q~)(\tilde{Q},\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}) we have volg~Q~​(ι⁡((−∞,0)×(V∗,0))):=∫ι⁡((−∞,0)×(V∗,0))−det​g~Q~<C\mathrm{vol}_{\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}}\left(\iota\left((-\infty,0)\times(V_{*},0)\right)\right):=\int_{\iota((-\infty,0)\times(V_{*},0))}\sqrt{-\text{det}\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}}<C for some constant CC. 4.2.1 Implications for strongly spherically symmetric extensions across the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon

As an example we consider the Reissner-Nordström black hole “interior” (MR​N,gR​N)(M_{RN},g_{RN}). This spacetime describes the interior (i.e. the region inside the event horizon) of a spherically symmetric black hole of mass MM and charge ee. We assume that M2>e2>0M^{2}>e^{2}>0 (i.e. the black hole is “sub-extremal”). Consider ℝ2×𝕊2\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} with global coordinates (u,v,θA=(θ,ϕ))(u,v,\theta^{A}=(\theta,\phi)) and

gR​N=−(r−r+)​(r−r−)2​r2​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)+r2​g𝕊2.g_{RN}=-\frac{(r-r_{+})(r-r_{-})}{2r^{2}}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+r^{2}\cancel{g}_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}. (66)

where r∈(r−,r+)r\in(r_{-},r_{+}) is defined implicitly by

v−u2\displaystyle\frac{v-u}{2} =r+12​κ+​log⁡(r+−rr+)+12​κ−​log⁡(r−r−r−)\displaystyle=r+\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}\log\left(\frac{r_{+}-r}{r_{+}}\right)+\frac{1}{2\kappa_{-}}\log\left(\frac{r-r_{-}}{r_{-}}\right) (67)
=:r∗​(r)\displaystyle=:r_{*}(r) (68)

The boundary r=r−r=r_{-} corresponds to a Cauchy horizon for the full Reissner-Nordström spacetime [13], while r=r+>r−r=r_{+}>r_{-} corresponds to the event horizon. In order to construct the reference extension across the Cauchy horizon we introduce Kruskal coordinates (U,V)∈Q=(−∞,0)×(−∞,0)(U,V)\in Q=(-\infty,0)\times(-\infty,0) defined by

U=−e−κ−​uV=−eκ−​v.U=-e^{-\kappa_{-}u}\quad V=-e^{\kappa_{-}v}. (69)

and the metric in these coordinates is

gR​N=−r+​r−2​κ−2​r2​e−2​κ−​r​(r+−rr+)1−κ−/κ+⏟=:ΩR​N2(dU⊗dV+dV⊗dU)⏟=:gQ+r2g𝕊2,g_{RN}=\underbrace{-\underbrace{\frac{r_{+}r_{-}}{2\kappa_{-}^{2}r^{2}}e^{-2\kappa_{-}r}\left(\frac{r_{+}-r}{r_{+}}\right)^{1-\kappa_{-}/\kappa_{+}}}_{=:\Omega_{RN}^{2}}\left(dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU\right)}_{=:g_{Q}}+r^{2}\cancel{g}_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}, (71)

where r⁡(U,V)r(U,V) is implicitly given by U​V=e2​κ−​r⋅(r+−rr+)κ−κ+​(r−r−r−)UV=e^{2\kappa_{-}r}\cdot\Big(\frac{r_{+}-r}{r_{+}}\Big)^{\frac{\kappa_{-}}{\kappa_{+}}}\Big(\frac{r-r_{-}}{r_{-}}\Big) . The reference extension across the ‘right’ Cauchy horizon is given by MR​N¯:=Q¯×𝕊2:=(−∞,0)×(−∞,0]×𝕊2\overline{M_{RN}}:=\overline{Q}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}:=(-\infty,0)\times(-\infty,0]\times\mathbb{S}^{2}. Indeed, the metric (71) extends analytically to {V=0}\{V=0\}.

Note that (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}) is a 1+1-dimensional Lorentzian manifold. Consider a C0C^{0}-extension ιQ:Q↪Q~\iota_{Q}:Q\hookrightarrow\tilde{Q} of QQ across {V=0}\{V=0\}, where the continuous Lorentzian metric on Q~\tilde{Q} is denoted by g~Q~\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}. Assume that rr extends as a continuous strictly positive function to Q~\tilde{Q}. We then set M~=Q~×𝕊2\tilde{M}=\tilde{Q}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} and, with slight abuse of notation, define the spherically symmetric Lorentzian metric g~=g~Q~+r2​g𝕊2\tilde{g}=\tilde{g}_{\tilde{Q}}+r^{2}\cancel{g}_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} on M~\tilde{M}. Then ι:=ιQ×i​d𝕊2:MR​N↪M~\iota:=\iota_{Q}\times id_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}:M_{RN}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is a C0C^{0}-extension of (MR​N,gR​N)(M_{RN},g_{RN}) across {V=0}\{V=0\}. C0C^{0}-extensions arising in such a way are called strongly spherically symmetric.

We now discuss the implications of the results obtained in this section for such strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extensions. First let us note that if we only consider a subregion of MR​NM_{RN} of finite UU, i.e.

MR​N∗=(U1,U2)×(−∞,0)⏟=:Q∗×𝕊2M_{RN}^{*}=\underbrace{(U_{1},U_{2})\times(-\infty,0)}_{=:Q^{*}}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}

for some −∞<U1<U2<0-\infty<U_{1}<U_{2}<0, then it follows from our Example 4.1 that one can construct a strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extension of MR​N∗M_{RN}^{*} across {V=0}\{V=0\} which terminates all outgoing null cones of constant UU in the same sphere! This uses crucially that the area radius rr of the spheres has a UU-independent limit for V→0V\to 0.

Example 4.5.

Consider (Q∗,gQ)(Q^{*},g_{Q}) with reference extension Q∗¯:=(U1,U2)×(−∞,0]\overline{Q^{*}}:=(U_{1},U_{2})\times(-\infty,0]. Note, moreover, that ΩR​N2\Omega^{2}_{RN} extends continuously to [U1,U2]×(−∞,0][U_{1},U_{2}]\times(-\infty,0]. As discussed in Section 4.2, there exists a C0C^{0}-extension ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β:Q∗↪Q~\iota_{corner,\beta}:Q^{*}\hookrightarrow\tilde{Q} with ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β​(U,0)=p~∈Q~\iota_{corner,\beta}(U,0)=\tilde{p}\in\tilde{Q} for all U∈(U1,U2)U\in(U_{1},U_{2}). Moreover, note that since rr extends continuously to [U1,U2]×(−∞,0][U_{1},U_{2}]\times(-\infty,0] with r⁡(U,0)=r−>0r(U,0)=r_{-}>0 for all U∈[U1,U2]U\in[U_{1},U_{2}], it follows from the construction in Example 4.1 that rr also extends as a continuous strictly positive function to Q~\tilde{Q}. Hence ι:=ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β×i​d𝕊2:MR​N∗↪M~:=Q~×𝕊2\iota:=\iota_{corner,\beta}\times id_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}:M_{RN}^{*}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}:=\tilde{Q}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} defines a strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extension which is not locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension MR​N∗¯:=(U1,U2)×(−∞,0]×𝕊2\overline{M_{RN}^{*}}:=(U_{1},U_{2})\times(-\infty,0]\times\mathbb{S}^{2}.

The next result uses Proposition 4.4 to show that one cannot globalise this corner construction to all of (MR​N,gR​N)(M_{RN},g_{RN}) because of the infinite spacetime volume between the event and Cauchy horizons. In particular, any strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extension of (MR​N,gR​N)(M_{RN},g_{RN}) across {V=0}\{V=0\} is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to the reference extension MR​N¯\overline{M_{RN}}.

Corollary 4.6 (Strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extensions of sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström across the Cauchy horizon).

Suppose ι=ιQ×i​d𝕊2:MR​N↪M~\iota=\iota_{Q}\times id_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}:M_{RN}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} is a strongly spherically symmetric C0C^{0}-extension of (MR​N,gR​N)(M_{RN},g_{RN}) across {V=0}\{V=0\} such that limV→0ιQ​(U∗,V)=p~\lim_{V\rightarrow 0}\iota_{Q}(U_{*},V)=\tilde{p} for some U∗∈(−∞,0)U_{*}\in(-\infty,0). Then there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that ιQ\iota_{Q} extends to [U∗−ϵ,U∗+ϵ]×(−ϵ,0][U_{*}-\epsilon,U_{*}+\epsilon]\times(-\epsilon,0] as a homeomorphism onto its image. In particular ι\iota is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to MR​N¯\overline{M_{RN}} at (U∗,0,ω0)∈MR​N¯(U_{*},0,\omega_{0})\in\overline{M_{RN}} for any ω0∈𝕊2\omega_{0}\in\mathbb{S}^{2}.

Proof.

We will show that volgQ​((−∞,0)×(V∗,0))=∞\mathrm{vol}_{g_{Q}}\left((-\infty,0)\times(V_{*},0)\right)=\infty for any V∗<0V_{*}<0, so that the result follows from Proposition 4.4. For U∗−1<V∗<V0<0U_{*}^{-1}<V_{*}<V_{0}<0, define (see Figure 16)

From (67) and (69), the condition U>V−1U>V^{-1} is equivalent to r∗>0r_{*}>0. Since r∗​(r)r_{*}(r) is strictly decreasing, it follows that for points in A⁡(V0)A(V_{0}) we have r−<r<r0r_{-}<r<r_{0}, where r0r_{0} is the unique solution to r∗​(r)=0r_{*}(r)=0 (so in particular is independent of V0V_{0}). We conclude from (71) that −det​gQ=ΩR​N2>C1>0\sqrt{-\mathrm{det}g_{Q}}=\Omega_{RN}^{2}>C_{1}>0 in A⁡(V0)A(V_{0}), where C1C_{1} is a constant independent of V0V_{0}. Using this, we have

volgQ​(A⁡(V0))=∫A⁡(V0)−det​gQ​dU​dV>C1​∫V∗V0(U∗−1V)​dV=C1​U∗​(V0−V∗)−C1​log⁡(V0​V∗−1)\begin{split}\mathrm{vol}_{g_{Q}}(A(V_{0}))&=\int_{A(V_{0})}\sqrt{-\mathrm{det}g_{Q}}\,dUdV>C_{1}\int_{V_{*}}^{V_{0}}\left(U_{*}-\frac{1}{V}\right)dV=C_{1}U_{*}(V_{0}-V_{*})-C_{1}\log\left(V_{0}V_{*}^{-1}\right)\end{split} (72)

It follows that for any V∗<0V_{*}<0 we have volgQ​(A⁡(V0))→∞\mathrm{vol}_{g_{Q}}(A(V_{0}))\rightarrow\infty as V0→0V_{0}\rightarrow 0, which then implies the claim. ∎

We remark that a similar argument also holds for the extremal case e=M>0e=M>0.

To summarise, we have shown that a finite UU-chunk of the interior of sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström does admit C0C^{0}-extensions with a different C0C^{0}-structure to the reference extension. In contrast, we have shown that the full spacetime does not admit such exotic C0C^{0}-extensions – at least if we restrict to strongly spherically symmetric extensions. We also briefly remark that if one considers small and generic perturbations of exact sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström initial data under the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system, then the Cauchy horizon turns into a spherically symmetric weak null singularity (see [18] and references therein). The spherically symmetric quotient (Q,gQ)(Q,g_{Q}) again admits a continuous reference extension as in the case of exact sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström and, furthermore, the area radius rr also extends continuously as a strictly positive function to the reference extension. However, in stark contrast to exact Reissner-Nordström, rr is generically no longer constant on the Cauchy horizon/weak null singularity, but is instead monotonically decreasing in UU [7, 17]. This even rules out our constructions of exotic C0C^{0}-extensions of finite UU-chunks!1616 16 Recall that the construction in Example 4.5 required limV→0r⁡(U,V)\lim_{V\to 0}r(U,V) to be independent of UU.

5 The C1C^{1}-Structure of Extensions in 1+1-Dimensions

5.1 Non-rigidity of the C1C^{1}-structure

We have seen in Section 4.1 how the requirement that the metric extends continuously imposes a certain rigidity on the C0C^{0}-structure of the extension. In particular, Theorem 4.3 outlines the two possible local C0C^{0}-structures: that of the corner extension and that of the reference extension. In this section we investigate whether the local C0C^{0}-structure is sufficient to determine the local C1C^{1}-structure. Example 5.1 shows that this is not the case if the C0C^{0}-structure is that of the corner. In Example 5.2 we show that it is also not the case if the C0C^{0}-structure is that of the reference extension. We thus conclude that the assumption of the metric extending continuously is not strong enough to give us rigidity properties on the C1C^{1}-structure of the extension.

Example 5.1.

For β,β′∈(12,1)\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in(\frac{1}{2},1) with β′>β\beta^{\prime}>\beta, let ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β:Mt↪M~t\iota_{corner,\beta}:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}_{t} and ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β′:Mt↪M~t\iota_{corner,\beta^{\prime}}:M_{t}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}_{t} be two corner extensions of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) into (M~t,g~β′)(\tilde{M}_{t},\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\beta}) and (M~t,g~β′′)(\tilde{M}_{t},\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\beta^{\prime}}) as described in Example 4.1. We claim that ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β\iota_{corner,\beta} and ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β′\iota_{corner,\beta^{\prime}} are C0C^{0}-equivalent but C1C^{1}-inequivalent extensions in the sense that the identification map i​d:ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β→ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β′id:\iota_{corner,\beta}\rightarrow\iota_{corner,\beta^{\prime}} defined by i​d:=ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β′∘ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β−1id:=\iota_{corner,\beta^{\prime}}\circ\iota_{corner,\beta}^{-1} extends to ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β​(Mt)¯⊂M~t\overline{\iota_{corner,\beta}(M_{t})}\subset\tilde{M}_{t} as a homeomorphism but not as a diffeomorphism.

The identification map is given in coordinates by

i​d​(p,q)=(p​|q|β′−β1−β,−|q|1−β′1−β)=:(p′​(p,q),q′​(p,q)).id(p,q)=\left(p|q|^{\frac{\beta^{\prime}-\beta}{1-\beta}},-|q|^{\frac{1-\beta^{\prime}}{1-\beta}}\right)=:(p^{\prime}(p,q),q^{\prime}(p,q)). (73)

This map extends as a homeomorphism to ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β​(Mt)¯={(p,q)∈(−1,1)×(−1,0]:|p|≤|q|β1−β}\overline{\iota_{corner,\beta}(M_{t})}=\{(p,q)\in(-1,1)\times(-1,0]:|p|\leq|q|^{\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}}\}. However, we have

∂qq′​(p,q)=1−β′1−β​|q|β−β′1−β→∞​ as ​q→0\begin{split}\partial_{q}q^{\prime}(p,q)&=\frac{1-\beta^{\prime}}{1-\beta}|q|^{\frac{\beta-\beta^{\prime}}{1-\beta}}\\ &\rightarrow\infty\text{ as }q\rightarrow 0\end{split} (74)

so i​did does not extend to ιc​o​r​n​e​r,β​(Mt)¯\overline{\iota_{corner,\beta}(M_{t})} as a diffeomorphism.

In the following example we construct a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mt,gt)(M_{t},g_{t}) which is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to Mt¯\overline{M_{t}} at (0,0)∈Mt¯(0,0)\in\overline{M_{t}} but not locally C1C^{1}-equivalent there.

5.2 Application to weak null singularities in 3+1-dimensions

Finally we return to our motivating example: weak null singularities (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) in 3+1-dimensions (see the beginning of the introduction). Example 5.2 can be used to construct a C0C^{0}-extension of (Mwns,gwns)(M_{\mathrm{wns}},g_{\mathrm{wns}}) which is locally C0C^{0}-equivalent to Mwns¯\overline{M_{\mathrm{wns}}} at (0,0,θA)(0,0,\theta^{A}) for any θA∈𝕊2\theta^{A}\in\mathbb{S}^{2} but not locally C1C^{1}-equivalent at these points.

Example 5.3.
